Use appropriate table markup (<thead>, <tbody>, <th>) to convey relationships programmatically.
Check that screen readers and keyboard navigation follow the same logical sequence as visually presented.
Use CSS for styling and positioning without disrupting the meaningful DOM order.
Place instructions for interactive controls immediately before or after the control in the DOM.
Test linearized reading order by disabling CSS or using a screen reader to confirm meaningful flow.
Use logical heading hierarchy (h1 → h2 → h3) so the sequence of information makes sense.
Ensure form instructions and error messages appear in a logical order and are programmatically associated with their fields.
Keep related content grouped together in the DOM (e.g., question text immediately before answer choices).
Ensure navigation menus and breadcrumbs follow a predictable, linearized order.
For responsive layouts, test both mobile and desktop breakpoints to confirm that content reflows in a logical order.
dont: Don’t rely solely on visual position; assistive technologies read based on DOM order.
Don’t use CSS properties like order, float, or absolute positioning to visually rearrange content in ways that break logical reading order.
Don’t reorder elements visually while leaving the DOM in an illogical or confusing sequence.
Don’t misuse structural elements (e.g., skipping heading levels or using list markup for non-list content).
Don’t use ARIA attributes to try to fix poor source order instead of correcting the DOM structure.
Don’t use non-semantic elements like <div> or <span> to fake structural roles (e.g., headings) without proper semantics.
Don’t insert content that appears visually first but comes last in the DOM hierarchy.
Don’t assume sighted users’ visual scanning order matches what assistive tech reads; always check DOM order.
Don’t break up sentences or paragraphs across multiple containers for styling only.
Don’t position labels or instructions visually without placing them correctly in the DOM.
Don’t rearrange DOM content dynamically with JavaScript in a way that causes assistive technology users to encounter content out of sequence.
Don’t rely on CSS pseudo-elements (::before/::after) to add meaningful content, since they aren’t always read by screen readers in the expected sequence.
edge_cases: Complex CSS Grid or Flexbox layouts may visually rearrange items in a different order than the DOM (e.g., using the 'order' property).
Multi-column layouts may cause the reading sequence to jump unexpectedly if columns are styled only with CSS.
Modal dialogs or dynamically injected content can disrupt the expected reading sequence if not correctly placed in the DOM.
Dynamically updated content in single-page applications may be inserted in the wrong logical sequence.
Long forms with grouped fields may appear visually logical but present an illogical tab or reading order if markup isn’t structured correctly.
The visual reading order differs from the source order, leading to confusing narration for screen readers.
Elements visually placed using layout or styling appear in a different order for keyboard or AT users.
Hidden or reordered content disrupts logical reading flow when made visible dynamically.
Automated systems detect DOM order but cannot interpret intended reading meaning or spatial flow.
Multi-column or responsive designs may shift reading sequence unpredictably across devices.
Content broken across multiple DOM elements affecting sequential reading.
Multi-line headings split into separate elements affecting comprehension.
